title: Dependency Management and Configuration
learning_outcomes: Explain how dependency management and configuration affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from dependencies and package managers to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on dependency management and configuration in backend architecture for rest apis. You will connect dependencies and package managers to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Dependency Management and Configuration matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying dependencies and package managers deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Separate request transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence so each responsibility can be tested independently. In this lesson, treat “Dependency Management and Configuration” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Dependencies and package managers”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Configuration by environment” and “Dependency locking and updates”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Keep controllers thin and make business rules testable without a live network request. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating dependency management and configuration. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.

Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.

content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Dependency Management and Configuration with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating dependency management and configuration as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
summary: Separate request transport, application use cases, domain rules, and persistence so each responsibility can be tested independently. In this lesson, treat “Dependency Management and Configuration” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.
Next, connect this idea to Lesson 100: Request Lifecycle and Context.
